title: The Giant Telescope That Spied on Soviet Missiles Might Be Shut Down Forever
summary: Picture a gigantic dish as tall as a 10-story building, pointing at the sky and listening to whispers from distant galaxies. That's the Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank Observatory in England. For almost 70 years, it's been a superstar of science—discovering new galaxies, training future astronomers, and even helping to keep an eye on Soviet missiles during the Cold War. But now, this iconic telescope might be forced to go silent. The UK's main science funding agency, UKRI, has decided to stop paying for scientific observations at Jodrell Bank starting April 1, 2028, unless new money is found. The cuts are part of a bigger plan to save money, and they'll also affect other big projects like the search for life on other planets. Scientists are furious. Professor Brian Cox, a famous physicist, called the decision "hasty and ill-considered" and said it's already damaged UK science. The closure would put 28 jobs at risk at the site, but it would also affect nearly 3,000 scientists worldwide who use Jodrell Bank's network of telescopes. The observatory is so important that it was named a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019. It's even appeared in pop culture, from "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" to "Doctor Who." Professor Simon Garrington, who works there, says Jodrell Bank is "a beacon for science" that inspires young people. He and others are fighting to find alternative funding to keep the Lovell Telescope running. They hope that this isn't the end of the story for a place that has stared into the universe and helped us understand our place in it.
why_it_matters: This telescope has inspired generations of kids to become scientists and helped us learn about space; if it goes silent, future discoveries might be lost, and young people might miss out on the wonder of the stars.

background_read: Jodrell Bank Observatory was founded in 1945 and the Lovell Telescope began working in 1957. At first, it tracked the first satellites and space probes, making Britain a leader in radio astronomy.
During the Cold War, the telescope secretly acted as an early warning system to detect Soviet nuclear missile tests, because its huge dish could pick up radio signals from far away.

In 2019, UNESCO (the United Nations organization that protects important cultural and natural sites) made Jodrell Bank a World Heritage site, recognising its huge impact on our understanding of the universe.

perspectives.description: They argue that Jodrell Bank is a world-leading research centre that trains astronomers and inspires future generations. Cutting its funding would harm UK science and break a chain of discovery that has lasted for decades.

It says it must make difficult choices to balance its budget and that other important science projects also need money. They believe new technology could eventually replace older telescopes like the Lovell.
